More mascots: when they first showed up.Quaker Oats man: The Ohio company claimed to be the first cereal trademark registered, and picked the Quaker name to suggest honesty and purity.
More mascots: when they first showed up.Morton Salt Girl: Her umbrella, plus the slogan when it rains it pours, advertised that Morton salt would not clump in damp weather.
More mascots: when they first showed up.Snap, Crackle & Pop (as elves): The three Rice Krispies characters were named for the cereal's sound in milk, and were first drawn as gnomes before elves.
More mascots: when they first showed up.Speedy Alka-Seltzer: Speedy, with an Alka-Seltzer tablet for a hat, was voiced for years by Dick Beals and starred in TV ads of the 1950s and 60s.
More mascots: when they first showed up.Trix Rabbit: The rabbit is forever tricked out of his cereal, and the cry silly rabbit, Trix are for kids has become a catchphrase.
More mascots: when they first showed up.Kool-Aid Man: He bursts through walls shouting oh yeah, advertising a drink invented in the 1920s by Edwin Perkins in Nebraska.
More mascots: when they first showed up.Chester Cheetah: The cool cheetah with sunglasses promotes Cheetos with the slogan it ain't easy being cheesy.
More mascots: when they first showed up.Taco Bell chihuahua: The little dog said yo quiero Taco Bell in ads and was voiced by Carlos Alazraqui, becoming a pop-culture sensation.
More mascots: when they first showed up.Aflac Duck: The company's name sounds like a duck's quack, so the ad agency made a duck mascot whose squawk became the brand's signature.
More mascots: when they first showed up.Flo from Progressive: Played by comedian Stephanie Courtney, a veteran of the Groundlings improv troupe, she became one of the longest-running ad characters in the US.

Screens by diagonal size.Smartwatch: Smartwatches pack a full computer, a heart rate sensor and a mobile connection into a screen small enough to wear on the wrist.
Screens by diagonal size.Smartphone: Most phones in this size range have screens that are measured diagonally, which helps compare displays of different shapes.
Screens by diagonal size.E-reader: E-readers use e-ink, which looks like paper and uses power only when the page changes, so batteries can last for weeks.
Screens by diagonal size.Tablet: Tablets sit between phones and laptops, and the first iPad launched in 2010 started the modern tablet market.
Screens by diagonal size.Laptop: Laptop screens are measured diagonally, and many are about this size because it balances portability and a comfortable view.
Screens by diagonal size.Desktop monitor: Monitors of this size are common on desks because they give a large work area at a short viewing distance.
Screens by diagonal size.Living-room TV: Television sets have grown larger as prices have fallen, and the typical size has gone up over the last decade.
Screens by diagonal size.Home projector screen: Home projectors can fill a wall, creating a cinema-like image, and are popular for movies and gaming.
Screens by diagonal size.Cinema screen: A cinema screen is measured by its width, and large halls often use a curved or very large flat screen.
Screens by diagonal size.IMAX screen: IMAX screens are enormous and often almost fill the viewer's field of vision, and they are designed to make films feel immersive.

Pirate history, in order.Drake raids Cádiz: He raided Cádiz and burned dozens of ships, 'singeing the King of Spain's beard' and delaying the Armada by a year.
Pirate history, in order.Henry Morgan sacks Panama: A Welsh privateer later made lieutenant governor of Jamaica, whose name lives on in a rum brand.
Pirate history, in order.Captain Kidd hanged: He was hanged at Execution Dock in London, and his body was displayed in a cage over the Thames.
Pirate history, in order.Blackbeard killed: Edward Teach was killed at Ocracoke Inlet by Lt. Robert Maynard, and his head was hung from the ship's bowsprit.
Pirate history, in order.Anne Bonny captured: Sailing with Calico Jack Rackham, she and Mary Read escaped execution by pleading pregnancy.
Pirate history, in order.Black Bart killed: Bartholomew Roberts captured over 400 vessels, among the most successful pirates ever, and was killed off West Africa.
Pirate history, in order.First Barbary War begins: The US's first foreign war after independence; the Marines' Hymn still mentions 'the shores of Tripoli'.
Pirate history, in order.Ching Shih surrenders: She commanded a huge fleet of pirates in the South China Sea, and retired with her fortune rather than being executed.
Pirate history, in order.Jean Lafitte at Galveston: He had helped Andrew Jackson defend New Orleans in 1815, then set up a base on Galveston Island.
Pirate history, in order.Maersk Alabama hijacked: Somali pirates seized the ship, and Captain Richard Phillips was freed by Navy SEAL snipers, inspiring the film Captain Phillips.

When these Japanese food firsts happened.MSG discovered: Kikunae Ikeda isolated it from kombu seaweed and named the taste umami.
When these Japanese food firsts happened.Calpis: Inspired by fermented milk from Mongolia, it blends milk and acid and its name blends calcium and a Sanskrit word.
When these Japanese food firsts happened.Kewpie mayonnaise: This Japanese mayo uses only egg yolks and rice vinegar, and has a baby doll mascot.
When these Japanese food firsts happened.Yakult: Dr. Minoru Shirota's probiotic is sold in tiny bottles.
When these Japanese food firsts happened.Conveyor-belt sushi: Its inventor got the idea from a beer bottling line's conveyor.
When these Japanese food firsts happened.Pocky: Glico's chocolate-coated stick is named for the sound of snapping, and November 11 is Pocky Day.
When these Japanese food firsts happened.Cup Noodles: Momofuku Ando invented instant ramen in 1958, and the cup came after he saw Westerners break noodles into cups.
When these Japanese food firsts happened.Hi-Chew: Morinaga's chewy candy is made to be an alternative to chewing gum.
When these Japanese food firsts happened.Pocari Sweat: Its name is not a real word and was picked simply because it sounded refreshing.
When these Japanese food firsts happened.Strong Zero: A shochu highball with citrus, this canned chu-hi is known for its 9 percent alcohol.

When these websites and apps launched.Amazon: It began in a garage in Washington state as an online bookstore, and one early name idea was Cadabra.
When these websites and apps launched.Google: Born from a Stanford research project, its name riffs on 'googol', the number 1 followed by 100 zeros.
When these websites and apps launched.Wikipedia: Founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger, this free encyclopedia now exists in over 300 languages.
When these websites and apps launched.Facebook: It began in a Harvard dorm room as 'Thefacebook', open at first only to Harvard students.
When these websites and apps launched.YouTube: The first video, 'Me at the zoo', runs 19 seconds and was uploaded by co-founder Jawed Karim.
When these websites and apps launched.Twitter: Its original 140-character limit was chosen to fit alongside a username inside a 160-character SMS text.
When these websites and apps launched.Instagram: It began as a check-in app called Burbn before pivoting to photos; Facebook bought it for about $1 billion in 2012.
When these websites and apps launched.Snapchat: It began as Picaboo, built by Stanford students around the hook that photos vanish after being viewed.
When these websites and apps launched.TikTok (global app): Its parent company merged it with Musical.ly in 2018; the Chinese sibling app Douyin had launched in 2016.
When these websites and apps launched.ChatGPT: It reached an estimated 100 million users in about two months, one of the fastest-growing apps ever.

Arabic letters, in standard alphabet ord.ا alif: Cognate with Hebrew aleph and Greek alpha, it is written as a simple vertical stroke.
Arabic letters, in standard alphabet ord.ب ba: It is one of the letters that change shape depending on position, with one dot beneath.
Arabic letters, in standard alphabet ord.ج jim: Related to Hebrew gimel, it has a dot below, and in Egyptian Arabic it is pronounced like a g.
Arabic letters, in standard alphabet ord.د dal: It does not connect to the next letter, and the abjad numeral system gave it the value 4.
Arabic letters, in standard alphabet ord.ر ra: It is a rolled or tapped sound, and one of six letters that do not connect to the following letter.
Arabic letters, in standard alphabet ord.س sin: Cognate with Hebrew shin, it begins the word salaam, peace.
Arabic letters, in standard alphabet ord.ص sad: It is one of the emphatic consonants, pronounced with the tongue pulled back.
Arabic letters, in standard alphabet ord.ع ayn: Ayn also means eye or spring, and its throat sound is hard for learners.
Arabic letters, in standard alphabet ord.ق qaf: Pronounced far back in the throat, it is a g in some dialects and a glottal stop in Cairo.
Arabic letters, in standard alphabet ord.ي ya: It is both a consonant and a long ee vowel, and the last letter of the alphabet.

Hours of sleep per day.Giraffe: Giraffes sleep in short bursts, sometimes only a few minutes at a time, and often doze standing up with their heads up.
Hours of sleep per day.Horse: Horses can sleep standing thanks to a locking mechanism in their legs, but they still need to lie down for real deep sleep.
Hours of sleep per day.Cow: Cows spend a lot of the day lying down chewing cud, but true sleep is relatively short, with REM sleep making up only a small part.
Hours of sleep per day.Human: Humans spend about a third of life asleep, and the brain uses that time to flush out waste products built up while awake.
Hours of sleep per day.Dog: Dogs sleep in phases and dream, and their twitching paws and muffled barks often come during REM sleep.
Hours of sleep per day.Cat: The word cat nap exists for a reason: housecats sleep most of the day, a leftover habit from hunting in short, exhausting bursts.
Hours of sleep per day.Platypus: The platypus is a monotreme that lays eggs, and it sleeps a lot, probably because its electric-sensing hunting is so demanding.
Hours of sleep per day.Tiger: A tiger sleeps so much because hunting takes huge energy, and it can sprint only briefly, so it rests long to save fuel.
Hours of sleep per day.Python: Pythons can sleep long hours, especially after a big meal, when digesting a large animal takes a great deal of their energy.
Hours of sleep per day.Little brown bat: Little brown bats hang upside down all day, entering torpor in winter, and spend most hours of each day asleep in roosts.

When these restaurant chains were founde.A&W: A&W is America's oldest franchised restaurant chain, and its name comes from its founders Allen and Wright.
When these restaurant chains were founde.White Castle: White Castle is credited with creating the hamburger chain concept, and its small square sliders inspired many imitators.
When these restaurant chains were founde.McDonald's: McDonald's began as a barbecue restaurant, and Ray Kroc later bought it and turned it into a global empire.
When these restaurant chains were founde.In-N-Out Burger: In-N-Out Burger started as the first drive-thru in California, and its menu is famously small, with a secret menu.
When these restaurant chains were founde.Dunkin': Dunkin' was founded in Quincy, Massachusetts, and it also appears in the doughnuts list, as its original name suggests.
When these restaurant chains were founde.Pizza Hut: Pizza Hut began in Wichita, Kansas, and it was founded by two brothers, who borrowed $600 from their mother.
When these restaurant chains were founde.Taco Bell: Taco Bell was founded by Glen Bell, and it popularized Mexican-inspired fast food across the United States.
When these restaurant chains were founde.Wendy's: Wendy's was named for founder Dave Thomas's daughter, and its square patties are meant to show that the burgers aren't cut corners.
When these restaurant chains were founde.Starbucks: Starbucks was named after the first mate in Moby-Dick, and it started in Seattle's Pike Place Market selling coffee beans.
When these restaurant chains were founde.Chipotle: Chipotle began in Denver, and its name comes from a smoked jalapeno chili, and it was funded in part by the founder's father.

German numbers, by the value they name.drei: Drei is three, and it is the first number in the list, and it sounds like the English word dry.
German numbers, by the value they name.sieben: Sieben means seven, and it is similar in sound to English seven, as both come from a common Germanic root.
German numbers, by the value they name.elf: Elf is eleven, and it's the same word as the English elf, though they have different meanings, as eleven comes from one left.
German numbers, by the value they name.zwölf: Zwolf means twelve, and it comes from two left, as does the English twelve.
German numbers, by the value they name.siebzehn: Siebzehn means seventeen, and it follows a regular pattern of adding zehn, meaning ten, to the units.
German numbers, by the value they name.zwanzig: Zwanzig means twenty, and German counts tens such as these differently than the English ty ending.
German numbers, by the value they name.vierzig: Vierzig is forty, and the German in the number-writing order puts units before tens in the numbers like 41.
German numbers, by the value they name.achtzig: Achtzig is eighty, and its t sound is shared with acht, meaning eight, which is why it seems to repeat the t.
German numbers, by the value they name.hundert: Hundert is a hundred, and it comes from a Germanic word, as does the English one.
German numbers, by the value they name.tausend: Tausend is a thousand, and the German word for million, Million, is a false friend of Milliarde which means a billion.

Cities by standard-time UTC offset.Honolulu: Honolulu is in Hawaii, which doesn't observe daylight saving time, and it is among the westernmost large US cities.
Cities by standard-time UTC offset.Los Angeles: Los Angeles is at UTC minus 8 in winter, and the entertainment industry there is why Pacific Time is often quoted for premieres.
Cities by standard-time UTC offset.New York: New York is on Eastern Time, and the city's stock exchange opens at 9:30 a.m. there.
Cities by standard-time UTC offset.São Paulo: Sao Paulo is Brazil's largest city, and Brazil abolished daylight saving time in 2019.
Cities by standard-time UTC offset.London: London sits on the Greenwich meridian, which defines 0 degrees longitude and the basis of world time.
Cities by standard-time UTC offset.Cairo: Cairo is at UTC plus 2, and Egypt reintroduced daylight saving time in 2023.
Cities by standard-time UTC offset.Moscow: Moscow stays at UTC plus 3 all year, as Russia abolished seasonal clock changes in 2014.
Cities by standard-time UTC offset.Mumbai: Mumbai is on India Standard Time, which is offset by a half hour, as the whole country uses one time zone.
Cities by standard-time UTC offset.Seoul: Seoul is at UTC plus 9, the same as Tokyo, and South Korea does not observe daylight saving time.
Cities by standard-time UTC offset.Auckland: Auckland is among the first major cities to see each new day, and New Zealand is at UTC plus 12 in winter.

Hindi numbers, by the value they name.ek: It comes from Sanskrit eka, and you can hear the root in ekta, meaning unity.
Hindi numbers, by the value they name.do: It is a distant cousin of English two, as well as Latin duo.
Hindi numbers, by the value they name.teen: It is related to English three and Latin tres, all cousins from the same ancient language.
Hindi numbers, by the value they name.chaar: A cousin of Latin quattuor, it comes from Sanskrit catur, as in the Sanskrit-derived chaturthi.
Hindi numbers, by the value they name.paanch: The Punjab region means land of five waters, a name built from the same number root.
Hindi numbers, by the value they name.chhah: It comes from Sanskrit shat, which is related to English six.
Hindi numbers, by the value they name.saat: From Sanskrit sapta, as in the Saptarishi, the seven sages of Hindu tradition.
Hindi numbers, by the value they name.aath: From Sanskrit ashta, as in Ashtanga yoga, eight limbs.
Hindi numbers, by the value they name.nau: It is a cousin of English nine and Latin novem, sharing a distant ancestor.
Hindi numbers, by the value they name.das: It comes from Sanskrit dasha; the Dussehra festival's name is linked to ten for the demon king Ravana's ten heads.

Sci-fi movie landmarks by release.Metropolis: Fritz Lang's silent epic of a class-divided city was among the most expensive films of its era, and a long-lost cut was partly rediscovered in Argentina in 2008.
Sci-fi movie landmarks by release.The Day the Earth Stood Still: A flying saucer lands in Washington, and the film's famous line 'Klaatu barada nikto' commands the robot Gort to stand down.
Sci-fi movie landmarks by release.2001: A Space Odyssey: Stanley Kubrick and Arthur C. Clarke made a film with little dialogue, and its slow spinning space station scenes were set to Strauss's waltz.
Sci-fi movie landmarks by release.Alien: Swiss artist H. R. Giger designed the film's xenomorph, and its tagline 'In space, no one can hear you scream' became one of cinema's best-known.
Sci-fi movie landmarks by release.Blade Runner: Ridley Scott's rain-soaked, neon-lit Los Angeles was adapted from Philip K. Dick's novel 'Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?'.
Sci-fi movie landmarks by release.The Terminator: James Cameron made this on under 7 million dollars, and its title cyborg, played by Schwarzenegger, speaks very few lines, the biggest being 'I'll be back'.
Sci-fi movie landmarks by release.The Matrix: The Wachowskis' film used 'bullet time' effects, with a ring of still cameras, to make Keanu Reeves dodge bullets in slow motion.
Sci-fi movie landmarks by release.Inception: Christopher Nolan's heist film about dreams within dreams used a spinning top as its ambiguous final image, and it won four Oscars.
Sci-fi movie landmarks by release.Interstellar: Christopher Nolan's space epic used physicist Kip Thorne's equations to render its black hole, which led to a scientific paper.
Sci-fi movie landmarks by release.Dune (Villeneuve): Denis Villeneuve adapted Frank Herbert's 1965 novel, which is often called the best-selling science fiction novel ever.

Surprising timeline: put these in order.Great Pyramid built: Great Pyramid of Giza was the tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years, and its builders were paid workers, not slaves, as discoveries of their town show.
Surprising timeline: put these in order.Last woolly mammoths die out: Isolated woolly mammoths on Wrangel Island survived until about 4,000 years ago, so some were still alive when the Great Pyramid had stood for centuries.
Surprising timeline: put these in order.Tutankhamun dies: The boy king died at about 19, and his tomb was found largely intact by Howard Carter in 1922, and its gold mask is famous.
Surprising timeline: put these in order.Rome founded (legend): Legend says Romulus founded the city after killing his twin Remus, and Romans celebrated this date, 21 April, as its birthday.
Surprising timeline: put these in order.Cleopatra dies: Egypt's last active pharaoh lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the Great Pyramid's construction, which stood about 2,500 years before her.
Surprising timeline: put these in order.Teaching begins at Oxford: Teaching at Oxford began around 1096 and makes it the oldest university in the English-speaking world, older than the Aztec capital.
Surprising timeline: put these in order.Genghis Khan born: Born as Temujin, he united the Mongol tribes, and legend says he was born clutching a blood clot, a sign of the destiny to come.
Surprising timeline: put these in order.Tenochtitlan founded: The Aztec capital was built on an island in Lake Texcoco, and today's Mexico City sits on its ruins.
Surprising timeline: put these in order.Machu Picchu built: Built high in the Andes for the Inca emperor Pachacuti, this citadel was brought to world attention by Hiram Bingham in 1911.
Surprising timeline: put these in order.Columbus reaches the Americas: Columbus reached the Caribbean, searching for Asia, and he believed to the end of his life that he had landed near it.

Mario Kart games, in order.Super Mario Kart: Super Mario Kart pioneered the kart-racing genre and used the SNES's Mode 7 to make flat tracks appear in 3D.
Mario Kart games, in order.Mario Kart 64: Mario Kart 64 introduced true 3D tracks and four-player split screen, which made it a staple of living rooms.
Mario Kart games, in order.Mario Kart: Super Circuit: Super Circuit for the Game Boy Advance included all the tracks from the original Super Mario Kart, as unlockable extras.
Mario Kart games, in order.Mario Kart: Double Dash!!: Double Dash!! let two characters share each kart, one driving and the other throwing items, which was unique in the series.
Mario Kart games, in order.Mario Kart DS: Mario Kart DS was the first in the series to offer online play over Nintendo's Wi-Fi Connection.
Mario Kart games, in order.Mario Kart Wii: Mario Kart Wii came with a plastic steering wheel accessory and sold over 37 million copies, one of the best-selling racing games ever.
Mario Kart games, in order.Mario Kart 7: Mario Kart 7 added gliders and underwater driving, and let players customize kart parts for the first time on a handheld.
Mario Kart games, in order.Mario Kart 8: Mario Kart 8 added anti-gravity sections where karts drive on walls and ceilings, and was later re-released on Switch with extra tracks.
Mario Kart games, in order.Mario Kart Tour: Mario Kart Tour was a mobile game that used a free-to-play model and a rotating schedule of city-inspired tracks.
Mario Kart games, in order.Mario Kart World: Mario Kart World, the Switch 2 launch title, shifted to an open world connecting tracks and allowing up to 24 players.

The Ten Commandments (Protestant numberi.No other gods: The first commandment forbids worshipping other gods, and it opens the list after God introduces himself as the one who freed Israel from slavery.
The Ten Commandments (Protestant numberi.No carved idols: The second forbids making carved images to worship, and some traditions count it together with the first.
The Ten Commandments (Protestant numberi.Don't misuse God's name: Misusing God's name covers more than swearing, and it includes false oaths.
The Ten Commandments (Protestant numberi.Keep the Sabbath holy: The Sabbath is the seventh day of rest, and its roots are in the creation story, where God rests on the seventh day.
The Ten Commandments (Protestant numberi.Honor your parents: This is the first commandment that deals with human relationships, and it comes with a promise of long life.
The Ten Commandments (Protestant numberi.Do not murder: The Hebrew verb used here is more specifically about unlawful killing than all killing.
The Ten Commandments (Protestant numberi.Do not commit adultery: Adultery is forbidden, and in the ancient world the law protected marriages and family.
The Ten Commandments (Protestant numberi.Do not steal: Some scholars think the commandment on stealing was originally about kidnapping, which carried a death penalty.
The Ten Commandments (Protestant numberi.No false witness: The ninth commandment is about false testimony in court, which was serious in a time when a lie might condemn someone to death.
The Ten Commandments (Protestant numberi.Do not covet: Coveting is the only commandment about thoughts rather than actions, and it forbids wanting a neighbor's house, spouse or property.

The human body in art and pop culture.Vitruvian Man: Leonardo da Vinci drew it to show the ideal proportions of the human body, based on the Roman architect Vitruvius.
The human body in art and pop culture.Rembrandt's Anatomy Lesson: Rembrandt's group portrait shows Dr Nicolaes Tulp dissecting a forearm for a rapt audience.
The human body in art and pop culture.Frankenstein: Mary Shelley began writing it at about 18, during a stormy summer in Switzerland.
The human body in art and pop culture.Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde: Robert Louis Stevenson reportedly wrote its first draft in days after a nightmare.
The human body in art and pop culture.Fantastic Voyage: Isaac Asimov wrote the novelization of this movie about a miniaturized submarine that travels through a human body.
The human body in art and pop culture.Once Upon a Time... Life: This French animated series explained how the body's systems work, created by Albert Barillé.
The human body in art and pop culture.Body Worlds exhibition: Gunther von Hagens's exhibition showed plastinated real human bodies, drawing both crowds and controversy.
The human body in art and pop culture.Osmosis Jones: This part-animated comedy follows a white blood cell, voiced by Chris Rock, inside a man's body.
The human body in art and pop culture.Grey's Anatomy (TV): The show is named for Gray's Anatomy, the famous medical textbook first published in 1858.
The human body in art and pop culture.Inside Out: Pixar's story shows five emotions in a girl's head, including Joy and Sadness.

Angles by size.Arcsecond: A coin viewed from several kilometers away spans about this much; astronomers measure star positions in these.
Angles by size.Arcminute: The Moon is about 30 of them across, and a nautical mile is one of them of latitude.
Angles by size.Milliradian: Used in rifle scopes, one of them spans about 10 centimeters at a distance of 100 meters.
Angles by size.Gradian: Also called a gon, it makes a right angle a tidy 100 units, handy in surveying in some countries.
Angles by size.Radian: The angle where the arc length equals the radius, it makes calculus formulas simple, so mathematicians prefer it.
Angles by size.Right angle: The corner of squares and carpentry; 'right' comes from the Latin rectus, 'upright'.
Angles by size.Water molecule bond angle: Water's bent shape makes it a polar molecule, which is key to its power as a solvent.
Angles by size.Methane bond angle: Its four hydrogens spread into a tetrahedron, the same angle seen in the structure of diamond.
Angles by size.Golden angle: The angle that governs how sunflower seeds and leaves pack efficiently, linked to the golden ratio.
Angles by size.Full turn: The 360 probably traces to the ancient Babylonians' base-60 counting and a year of roughly 360 days.

Famous dogs, real and fictional, by year.Toto (Oz book): Dorothy's little black dog in L. Frank Baum's novel; the 1939 film cast a Cairn terrier named Terry, who was later renamed Toto.
Famous dogs, real and fictional, by year.Balto's serum run: The Siberian husky who led the last leg of the relay carrying diphtheria antitoxin to Nome, Alaska. His statue stands in New York's Central Park.
Famous dogs, real and fictional, by year.Pluto (Disney): Oddly, Mickey's pet is a dog who walks on all fours and never speaks, while Goofy, another dog, walks upright and wears clothes.
Famous dogs, real and fictional, by year.Hachiko dies: The Akita who kept returning to Tokyo's Shibuya Station for about nine years, waiting for his late owner. His bronze statue is now a famous meeting spot.
Famous dogs, real and fictional, by year.Lassie (first film): Lassie is a female collie in the story, but the film role went to a male dog named Pal, whose fuller coat looked better on camera.
Famous dogs, real and fictional, by year.Snoopy: Charlie Brown's beagle first appeared in Peanuts in October 1950, and he gradually grew from a plain pup into a daydreaming World War I flying ace.
Famous dogs, real and fictional, by year.Laika in orbit: The Moscow street dog aboard Sputnik 2 became the first animal to orbit Earth. The mission was designed with no return, a sad fact of early spaceflight.
Famous dogs, real and fictional, by year.Clifford the Big Red Dog: Norman Bridwell's picture books about a giant red dog began in 1963. Clifford is often described as about 25 feet tall, yet his owner is a small girl.
Famous dogs, real and fictional, by year.Scooby-Doo: The name reportedly came from the scat line "scooby-dooby-doo" in Frank Sinatra's song Strangers in the Night, which struck a CBS executive.
Famous dogs, real and fictional, by year.Odie (Garfield): Garfield's slobbering yellow dog started out in the 1978 strip as the pet of Garfield's roommate Lyman, before Jon Arbuckle took him in.

Hours ahead of UTC: Asia and Australia.Dubai: The UAE has no daylight saving time, so Dubai stays four hours ahead of UTC all year.
Hours ahead of UTC: Asia and Australia.Karachi: Pakistan sits five hours ahead of UTC and has experimented with daylight saving time, though it doesn't use it now.
Hours ahead of UTC: Asia and Australia.New Delhi: India uses a single zone, a half-hour off the hour grid, for a country that stretches across nearly 30 degrees of longitude.
Hours ahead of UTC: Asia and Australia.Kathmandu: Nepal's unusual 45-minute offset was adopted in 1986, making it one of the few places not on a half-hour grid.
Hours ahead of UTC: Asia and Australia.Dhaka: Bangladesh's capital is six hours ahead, and the country briefly used daylight saving in 2009.
Hours ahead of UTC: Asia and Australia.Bangkok: Thailand's capital sits seven hours ahead, and the country has no daylight saving time.
Hours ahead of UTC: Asia and Australia.Beijing: China uses just one time zone across the whole country, so western regions have a very late sunrise.
Hours ahead of UTC: Asia and Australia.Tokyo: Japan's standard time is nine hours ahead, and it's anchored on a meridian passing through Akashi.
Hours ahead of UTC: Asia and Australia.Adelaide (standard): South Australia sets its standard time half an hour behind the east coast, and its clocks change in summer.
Hours ahead of UTC: Asia and Australia.Sydney (standard): Australia's largest city is on UTC+10 in winter and moves its clocks forward in summer, unlike Brisbane next door.

Big acquisitions: what the buyer paid.Instagram (Facebook): Instagram had only 13 employees when it was bought in 2012, which in hindsight looks like a bargain.
Big acquisitions: what the buyer paid.YouTube (Google): Less than two years after it was founded, it was bought for shares, and became the foundation of Google's video empire.
Big acquisitions: what the buyer paid.Mojang (Microsoft): Markus 'Notch' Persson created Minecraft, the best-selling video game of all time, and later left the company.
Big acquisitions: what the buyer paid.Marvel (Disney): The deal came before the Avengers films made Marvel a box-office giant, and it brought Spider-Man into the family.
Big acquisitions: what the buyer paid.Pixar (Disney): The deal made Steve Jobs Disney's biggest shareholder, and brought Toy Story's creators into the fold.
Big acquisitions: what the buyer paid.Whole Foods (Amazon): It was Amazon's biggest purchase and put it into physical supermarkets, with hundreds of stores.
Big acquisitions: what the buyer paid.WhatsApp (Facebook): WhatsApp had only a few dozen engineers when it was bought, but served hundreds of millions of users.
Big acquisitions: what the buyer paid.LinkedIn (Microsoft): It was Microsoft's largest purchase at the time, and brought it a giant network of professionals.
Big acquisitions: what the buyer paid.Twitter (Musk): Renamed X in 2023, the platform was taken private at this price in a deal that began as a tweet.
Big acquisitions: what the buyer paid.Activision (Microsoft): Microsoft's largest deal ever, it brought Call of Duty and Candy Crush, through King, under one roof.

Newspaper comic strips, by debut.The Yellow Kid: Richard Outcault's bald child in a yellow nightshirt was among the first colour comics, and rival papers' fight over him is said to have coined 'yellow journalism'.
Newspaper comic strips, by debut.Little Nemo: Winsor McCay's dreamlike strip, full of enormous beds and sprawling landscapes, ended every episode with its hero waking up.
Newspaper comic strips, by debut.Krazy Kat: George Herriman's surreal strip had Ignatz the mouse hurl bricks at Krazy, who took them as signs of love. Poet E. E. Cummings admired it.
Newspaper comic strips, by debut.Popeye (Thimble Theatre): Popeye joined E. C. Segar's strip as a minor sailor in 1929 and took over. His spinach habit reportedly lifted real spinach sales.
Newspaper comic strips, by debut.Dick Tracy: Chester Gould's detective used a two-way wrist radio years before such gadgets existed, and faced grotesque villains such as Flattop.
Newspaper comic strips, by debut.Peanuts: Charles Schulz drew nearly 18,000 strips himself over almost 50 years and never used an assistant for the art.
Newspaper comic strips, by debut.Doonesbury: In 1975 Garry Trudeau became the first comic strip artist to win a Pulitzer Prize.
Newspaper comic strips, by debut.Garfield: Jim Davis named the cat after his grandfather, and the strip became one of the most widely syndicated comics in history.
Newspaper comic strips, by debut.Calvin and Hobbes: Bill Watterson named it after a theologian and a philosopher, ended it at its peak in 1995, and refused to license merchandise.
Newspaper comic strips, by debut.Dilbert: Scott Adams drew it while working at a phone company, and its pointy-haired boss became shorthand for clueless management.

Albert Einstein's life, in order.Born in Ulm: The family moved to Munich the following year, so he had no lasting ties to his birthplace in southern Germany.
Albert Einstein's life, in order.Joins the Swiss patent office: He worked as a technical examiner in Bern, a job he later called his 'worldly cloister', where he found time to think.
Albert Einstein's life, in order.Miracle-year papers: In 1905 he published four groundbreaking papers, on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity and E=mc².
Albert Einstein's life, in order.Moves to Berlin: He took a research post at the Prussian Academy of Sciences, just before World War I began, and opposed the war.
Albert Einstein's life, in order.General relativity: His new theory described gravity as curved spacetime, and explained a long-standing oddity in Mercury's orbit.
Albert Einstein's life, in order.Eclipse proves him right: Arthur Eddington's expedition measured starlight bending around the Sun, and the news made Einstein world-famous overnight.
Albert Einstein's life, in order.Nobel Prize year: The prize went to him for the photoelectric effect, not relativity, which the committee still thought too controversial.
Albert Einstein's life, in order.Moves to the United States: He left Germany as the Nazis rose to power, and took a post at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton.
Albert Einstein's life, in order.Letter to Roosevelt: Written largely by physicist Leo Szilard and signed by Einstein, it warned that Germany might build an atomic bomb.
Albert Einstein's life, in order.Dies in Princeton: He declined surgery for a burst aorta, reportedly saying he wanted to go when he wanted, and died in hospital at 76.

Words coined by famous writers and think.Utopia: More built the word from Greek for 'no place', and it may also pun on 'good place', so the joke sits inside the name.
Words coined by famous writers and think.Pandemonium: Milton named Satan's capital in Paradise Lost this, from Greek for 'all demons'. It now means any chaotic uproar.
Words coined by famous writers and think.Lilliputian: Swift's Gulliver's Travels gave the tiny people of Lilliput, about six inches tall, to English as a word for the very small.
Words coined by famous writers and think.Serendipity: Walpole coined it from a Persian fairy tale about the Three Princes of Serendip, an old name for Sri Lanka.
Words coined by famous writers and think.Chortle: Carroll's 'Jabberwocky' blended chuckle and snort into this word, one of his nonsense coinings that stuck.
Words coined by famous writers and think.Robotics: Asimov used it in a 1941 story, reportedly unaware he had named a real field of engineering.
Words coined by famous writers and think.Doublethink: From Nineteen Eighty-Four, it means holding two contradictory beliefs at once and accepting both.
Words coined by famous writers and think.Catch-22: Joseph Heller's novel was nearly titled Catch-18, but the number changed to avoid clashing with another book.
Words coined by famous writers and think.Meme: Richard Dawkins coined it in The Selfish Gene, shortening a Greek word for 'imitated thing', for ideas that spread between minds.
Words coined by famous writers and think.Cyberspace: William Gibson coined it in a 1982 short story, then made it famous with his novel Neuromancer two years later.

Waiting for baby: gestation times.Brown rat: Rats can breed within weeks of birth, which, combined with a short pregnancy, explains why populations can explode so quickly.
Waiting for baby: gestation times.European hedgehog: Baby hedgehogs, called hoglets, are born with soft spines hidden under swollen skin, which harden within a few days.
Waiting for baby: gestation times.Gray squirrel: North American gray squirrels were brought to Britain in the 1870s and have since pushed the native red squirrel to the margins.
Waiting for baby: gestation times.Red fox: The red fox has the widest range of any wild land carnivore, living on every continent except Antarctica and South America.
Waiting for baby: gestation times.Guinea pig: Guinea pig pups are born furry, with open eyes, and can nibble solid food within days, unlike most baby rodents.
Waiting for baby: gestation times.Tiger: Tiger cubs are born blind, and no two tigers share the same stripes, which are patterned on the skin as well as the fur.
Waiting for baby: gestation times.White-tailed deer: Fawns are born spotted and nearly scentless, which helps them hide from predators while the mother stays at a distance.
Waiting for baby: gestation times.Gorilla: A newborn gorilla weighs only about 2 kg, so tiny that it is fully dependent on its mother's grip for months.
Waiting for baby: gestation times.Bottlenose dolphin: Dolphin calves are born tail first and must swim to the surface for their first breath, often helped by their mother.
Waiting for baby: gestation times.White rhino: White rhinos are among the largest land mammals, yet the calf can stand within hours and trots beside its mother soon after.

How many parts a contest is split into.Halves in a soccer match: Each half is 45 minutes plus stoppage time. Knockout games that remain tied add extra time of two 15-minute halves.
How many parts a contest is split into.Periods in ice hockey: Three periods of 20 minutes, but because the clock stops on every whistle, a game usually takes over two hours.
How many parts a contest is split into.Quarters in an NBA game: Each quarter lasts 12 minutes, while men's college basketball uses two 20-minute halves.
How many parts a contest is split into.Max sets, men's Slam match: Matches are best of five sets. In 2010 John Isner and Nicolas Mahut's Wimbledon match lasted over 11 hours, with a final set ending 70-68.
How many parts a contest is split into.Innings in baseball: Nine innings, but a tie keeps the game going indefinitely. Little League games play only six.
How many parts a contest is split into.Frames in ten-pin bowling: A perfect game is 12 strikes in a row, worth 300 points, even though the game only has ten frames.
How many parts a contest is split into.Rounds in a title bout: Men's world title fights were 15 rounds until 1982, when the death of Duk Koo Kim led to a cut to 12.
How many parts a contest is split into.Days of a sumo tournament: Six grand tournaments a year each last 15 days, and a wrestler who wins eight bouts secures a winning record.
How many parts a contest is split into.Holes in a golf round: The standard was set after St Andrews cut its course from 22 holes to 18 in 1764.
How many parts a contest is split into.Stages of the Tour de France: Usually held over 23 days with two rest days, so it runs a stage a day for about three weeks.

Milestones in genetics.Chromosomes named: Walther Waldeyer coined the term in 1888. It means 'colored bodies' because they take up dyes under a microscope.
Milestones in genetics.Griffith's transformation: Frederick Griffith found that harmless bacteria could become deadly after meeting dead dangerous ones, hinting at a 'transforming principle'.
Milestones in genetics.DNA shown to carry genes: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed that DNA, not protein, is what carries heredity.
Milestones in genetics.Double helix: Watson and Crick built the model, using X-ray images by Rosalind Franklin, and shared a 1962 Nobel Prize.
Milestones in genetics.Recombinant DNA: Cohen and Boyer spliced a gene from one organism into bacteria, launching the biotechnology industry.
Milestones in genetics.Sanger sequencing: Frederick Sanger's method for reading DNA letters won him a second chemistry Nobel in 1980.
Milestones in genetics.DNA fingerprinting: Alec Jeffreys developed it in Leicester, and it soon helped solve real murder cases.
Milestones in genetics.Dolly the sheep: The first mammal cloned from an adult cell. Born at Scotland's Roslin Institute, she lived to about six.
Milestones in genetics.Human genome completed: The project began in 1990, with a draft in 2000. It spelled out about 3 billion letters of DNA.
Milestones in genetics.CRISPR gene editing: Doudna and Charpentier adapted a bacterial defence system into a gene editor and won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

When these sports joined the Olympics.Swimming: The first modern Games in Athens in 1896 held swimming in open water, in the chilly Bay of Zea, rather than in a pool.
When these sports joined the Olympics.Football (soccer): Soccer joined at the 1900 Paris Games, where a British club side, Upton Park FC, won the first gold.
When these sports joined the Olympics.Ice hockey: It debuted at the 1920 Antwerp Games, with Canada winning gold, years before the Winter Olympics even existed.
When these sports joined the Olympics.Basketball: Dr James Naismith invented the sport in 1891, and it debuted at the 1936 Berlin Games, played on outdoor courts.
When these sports joined the Olympics.Judo: Judo debuted in Tokyo, where Japan won three of the four golds, and Dutch giant Anton Geesink won the open class.
When these sports joined the Olympics.Beach volleyball: Born on California beaches, it joined the Games in Atlanta, where players compete barefoot on sand.
When these sports joined the Olympics.Snowboarding: It joined at the 1998 Nagano Games, where Canada's Ross Rebagliati won the first gold, and nearly lost it over cannabis traces.
When these sports joined the Olympics.Taekwondo: A Korean martial art known for fast, high kicks, it became a full medal sport at the Sydney Games.
When these sports joined the Olympics.Skateboarding: Delayed to 2021 by the pandemic, it debuted in Tokyo and produced medallists as young as 13.
When these sports joined the Olympics.Breaking: Breakdancing made its Olympic debut in Paris, and its athletes are called B-boys and B-girls.

Human family tree: who appeared first?.Sahelanthropus: Found in Chad in 2001 and nicknamed 'Toumai', its skull mixes ape-like and human-like features, and it may be our oldest relative.
Human family tree: who appeared first?.Orrorin: Its name means 'original man', and fossils found in Kenya in 2000 suggest it may have walked upright on two legs.
Human family tree: who appeared first?.Ardipithecus ramidus: The partial skeleton nicknamed Ardi, found in Ethiopia, shows a creature that could both climb trees and walk upright.
Human family tree: who appeared first?.Australopithecus afarensis: Its most famous fossil, Lucy, was found in Ethiopia in 1974 and stood only about 1.1 meters tall.
Human family tree: who appeared first?.Paranthropus: This 'nutcracker' hominin had huge molars and a crest on its skull to anchor powerful chewing muscles.
Human family tree: who appeared first?.Homo habilis: Its name means 'handy man', and fossils found in Tanzania were discovered with simple stone tools.
Human family tree: who appeared first?.Homo erectus: The first of our relatives with body proportions like ours, it spread out of Africa across Asia and may have used fire.
Human family tree: who appeared first?.Homo heidelbergensis: Named from a jaw found near Heidelberg, Germany, it may be a common ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans.
Human family tree: who appeared first?.Neanderthals: Our closest cousins lived across Europe and western Asia, and many people today carry a small percentage of their DNA.
Human family tree: who appeared first?.Homo sapiens: Our own species is old: fossils found at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco date back about 300,000 years.

Famous people who got patents, by year g.Abraham Lincoln: He is the only US president to hold a patent, for a device to lift boats over shoals. It was never actually built.
Famous people who got patents, by year g.Mark Twain: His patent was for an adjustable strap to hold clothes, but a self-pasting scrapbook from 1873 earned him more.
Famous people who got patents, by year g.Lillian Russell: The famed stage star patented a dresser-trunk combination, a practical design for her many touring costumes.
Famous people who got patents, by year g.Harry Houdini: The escape artist patented a diver's suit that allowed a wearer to escape from underwater quickly.
Famous people who got patents, by year g.Albert Einstein: Together with physicist Leo Szilard he developed a refrigerator that had no moving parts, hoping to prevent leaks of toxic gases.
Famous people who got patents, by year g.Hedy Lamarr: With composer George Antheil she patented a frequency-hopping signal system, and the idea later underpinned Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
Famous people who got patents, by year g.Zeppo Marx: The Marx Brother was also an engineer, and was granted a patent for a wristwatch-style pulse rate monitor.
Famous people who got patents, by year g.Eddie Van Halen: The guitarist patented a folding support that lets a player hold the instrument in unusual positions on stage.
Famous people who got patents, by year g.Jamie Lee Curtis: The actress patented a baby diaper with a built-in pocket for wipes, a rare patent from a film star.
Famous people who got patents, by year g.Michael Jackson: The singer patented shoes with a slot that let wearers lean far forward, as in the stage moves in 'Smooth Criminal'.

Islands by area.Cyprus: Cyprus is a Mediterranean island with a hotly disputed border, divided since 1974. Legend says Aphrodite rose from the sea near Paphos.
Islands by area.Sicily: The Mediterranean's largest island has Mount Etna, Europe's most active volcano. Greeks, Arabs and Normans each left their mark here.
Islands by area.Ireland: Ireland has no native snakes, and the island is the third largest in Europe. It's split between the Republic and Northern Ireland.
Islands by area.Iceland: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart. Nearly all its electricity comes from hydro and geothermal sources.
Islands by area.Great Britain: Great Britain is the largest island in Europe and the ninth largest in the world. England, Scotland and Wales all share it.
Islands by area.Sumatra: Home to orangutans and tigers found nowhere else, Sumatra sits in Indonesia. Its rainforests are some of the most threatened on Earth.
Islands by area.Madagascar: Madagascar split from the mainland about 88 million years ago, so most of its wildlife is unique. This includes all of the lemurs.
Islands by area.Borneo: This island is divided among three countries: Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. Its rainforest is older than the Amazon.
Islands by area.New Guinea: The world's second-largest island is split between Indonesia and Papua New Guinea. Papua New Guinea alone has over 800 languages.
Islands by area.Greenland: Greenland is the largest island that isn't a continent. An ice sheet covers about 80% of it, and holds enough water to raise sea level by over 7 metres.

TV and radio quiz shows, by debut.Information Please: A radio panel show where listeners mailed in questions to stump the experts, with prizes for those who did.
TV and radio quiz shows, by debut.Twenty-One: Contestants were secretly given answers, and Charles Van Doren's scandal inspired the 1994 film Quiz Show.
TV and radio quiz shows, by debut.University Challenge: It was first hosted by Bamber Gascoigne, famed for the phrase Your starter for ten, and the show is still going.
TV and radio quiz shows, by debut.Jeopardy!: Created by Merv Griffin, it asks answers and wants questions in reply; Alex Trebek hosted for decades.
TV and radio quiz shows, by debut.Family Feud: Players guess the top answers from surveys of 100 people, and Richard Dawson, the first host, famously kissed contestants.
TV and radio quiz shows, by debut.Who Wants to Be a Millionaire: It made Chris Tarrant famous with Is that your final answer?, and the format sold to dozens of countries.
TV and radio quiz shows, by debut.The Weakest Link: Anne Robinson's icy catchphrase, You are the weakest link. Goodbye., made her a star.
TV and radio quiz shows, by debut.QI: Stephen Fry's Quite Interesting show awards points for interesting answers, and a klaxon sounds for obvious but wrong ones.
TV and radio quiz shows, by debut.The Chase: Contestants face a professional quizzer called the Chaser, and Mark Labbett, known as the Beast, is a standout.
TV and radio quiz shows, by debut.HQ Trivia: A live mobile quiz with cash prizes, it peaked at over a million players at once before fading.
